tagline.text: A roughly 1 km wet cave traverse through the Palaopao Range in Bukidnon

location.label: Location
location.text: Entrance at Sitio Kilabong, Sumilao, Bukidnon · exit at Sitio Diamante, Dalirig, Manolo Fortich

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~900 (transport, entrance fee, guide and helmet, per person)

children.text: Sumalsag Cave is one of five caves in Bukidnon's Palaopao Range. It is an entrance-to-exit traverse of about 1.04 km that you walk, crawl and swim through along an underground stream. A guide and proper gear are needed for this adventure route.

Sumalsag Cave lies in the Palaopao Range of Bukidnon province in northern Mindanao, Philippines. Five caves are known in this range, and Sumalsag is the one most often recommended to travelers. It is said to be about

long, and you move through it by wading, crawling and sometimes swimming along an underground stream. Its defining trait is that it is not a sightseeing cave but a spelunking route you pass through with your whole body.

The cave is a traverse: you enter at one end and come out at the other. The usual route goes in at Sitio Kilabong in Vista Villa, Sumilao, and out at Sitio Diamante in Dalirig, Manolo Fortich. Because it spans two municipalities, some sources describe it as a Sumilao cave and others as a Manolo Fortich cave, but they mean the same cave. Knowing that the entrance and exit are in different villages makes it easier to plan transport.

Inside you will find an underground river, rock formations such as pillar-like stalagmites and stalactites, and narrow passages where you must crouch and duck-walk. Reviewers describe it as wet almost from start to finish. There are deep stretches where you must swim, slippery rocks to climb, and sections where bat guano covers the floor. At the end there is a narrow exit you must pass by submerging in water, and the pool beyond it is described as a reward for the effort.

It is also appealing as a day trip from Cagayan de Oro. However, the fees and conditions in this guide partly rely on reviews from several years ago, so please confirm the latest status with the local government and your guide before you go. It may not suit those who swim poorly, dislike enclosed spaces, or expect a light stroll with the family. For anyone who enjoys finding their way through water and darkness, though, it is one of Bukidnon's standout adventures. As for preparation, keeping your load light is key. Put a change of clothes, a towel, water and snacks in one dry bag, and wear only clothes that can get wet and non-slip footwear. Cotton jeans get heavy and restrict movement when wet, so quick-drying sportswear is better. The guide will tell you where to grip and what posture to use in each section, so rather than chasing photos, follow the guide's instructions one step at a time. It is safer and often more fun.

blocks.title: A wet cave along an underground river

children.text: Water flows along the cave floor, and its depth varies from ankle to neck level depending on the section. One reviewer described it as a cave that is wet from beginning to end. The water is cold, so keep body temperature in mind.
In places the ceiling is low and you must stoop or crawl on your belly. Some reviews say larger people may find it hard to get through, so it is wise to talk it over with your guide beforehand.
Shine your headlamp and you will see rock standing like columns and smoothly worn walls. In places sharp rock hangs low overhead, so a helmet is a must.

blocks.title: The final exit through the water

children.text: The exit is narrow and is said to require submerging your body to pass. Outside there is a clear pool where you can catch your breath. A dry bag is especially useful in this section.

blocks.title: Five caves in the Palaopao Range

children.text: Five caves are known in this range, and Sumalsag is the best known among them. Travel guides to caving in Bukidnon mention it often.

You register in the entrance village of Kilabong and go in with a local guide. The entrance and guide fees go back to the community, and one review says you could borrow a resident's tap to wash up after leaving the cave.

items.title: Day route from Cagayan de Oro
items.subtitle: A cave trip by bus and motorcycle taxi

children.text: Take a provincial bus toward Valencia or other southbound destinations from the bus terminal in Cagayan de Oro. Tell the driver in advance that you are getting off at Dalirig. The ride is said to take about
1 hour 20 minutes

Register at the Goay residence next to the Catholic church in Kilabong, and arrange your entrance fee, guide and helmet. Also check your headlamp, dry bag, swimwear and a change of clothes.

Pass through by walking, crawling and swimming along the underground river. Take photos slowly and only when you can get the camera out of the dry bag.
Pass through the narrow exit under the water and come out at Sitio Diamante. Borrow water from a resident near the exit to wash up and change clothes.
Take a motorcycle taxi to the main road at Dalirig and wait for a bus. Take a bus toward Cagayan de Oro or Malaybalay.
Reviews differ on how long the trip takes, so do not schedule anything else late in the afternoon and leave some slack. After rain the water rises, so it is safer to postpone.

Sumalsag is a cave with an underground stream, so heavy rain raises the water level and makes the way slippery. It is therefore safer to go in the relatively dry months. Bukidnon is highland, however, and has rainy days all year round, so give priority to the weather on the day and your guide's judgment.

The water inside is cold regardless of the outside temperature. On a hot day it feels refreshing, but staying in the water for long lowers your body temperature. A schedule that starts early in the morning, finishes by midday, and lets you wash up and change in the village works well.

There are almost no lodgings or restaurants in the entrance village of Kilabong or the exit village of Diamante, so it is more realistic to stay in Cagayan de Oro or Malaybalay. Cagayan de Oro has plenty of lodging and restaurants and is close to the airport, while Malaybalay is the center of Bukidnon and works well for combining other sights.

Eat lightly before the trip and bring plenty of water. A full stomach makes the narrow passages uncomfortable. It is hard to take out and eat food inside the cave, so a simple energy bar in the dry bag is enough. Afterward, eat at a small eatery along the Dalirig main road or back in town.
Returning to Cagayan de Oro, you can finish the day with local food in the city. The cave experience is tiring, so avoid cramming other plans into the same day.
Always enter with a local guide. The cave is dark and it is easy to get lost.
A dry bag is close to essential. Put in anything that must not get wet; it is also said to work as a floating aid in deep water.
Bring a headlamp and spare batteries. A handheld flashlight is awkward because your hands are not free.
If you swim poorly, bring a life vest or float and tell your guide beforehand.
Wear non-slip water shoes or sandals with sturdy soles. Flip-flops can come off.
Bring a towel and a separate change of clothes, and ask a resident for permission before you wash up after the cave.
It is safest to put your phone and camera in waterproof cases or leave them behind.
If you are large or claustrophobic, the narrow sections may be hard, so discuss this beforehand.
Before setting out, ask your guide about the signals used inside the cave and where you will rest. In a group, move at the pace of the person at the back to stay safe.
Do not enter after rain or on a day when rain is forecast, because the water can rise and become very dangerous.
Deep-water sections and narrow crawl sections make it dangerous for people who cannot swim or who are in poor health.
Sharp rock overhead and on the walls can injure you if you go in without a helmet.
The floor is slippery and in places has bat guano, so grip firmly with hands and feet.
Fees, contact numbers and registration methods come from reviews several years old and may have changed. Check the latest notices from the Manolo Fortich and Sumilao local governments.
Never explore alone, and be sure to be out before dark.
